title: Single-sided unbalanced addLiquidity into sUSDS/phUSD Balancer V3 pool is MEV-extractable; caller-supplied minBPT is the only defence and there is no fresh on-chain quote
description:
pool(uint256 minBPT, uint256 minUSDC) calls IBalancerVault.addLiquidity with AddLiquidityKind.UNBALANCED, passing only sUSDS on one side (and 0 on the other). Balancer V3 mathematically prices a single-sided UNBALANCED add as if the joiner first swapped half of the deposit through the pool to balance it, charging a swap fee on the implied imbalance, and then performs a proportional add. This means the BPT returned is highly sensitive to the pool's current sUSDS/phUSD spot price (i.e., the same as a swap). The only protection in the contract is the caller-supplied minBPT. The contract exposes getIdealBPT() for off-chain quoting, but: (1) it is NOT called atomically inside pool(); (2) it is computed before the transaction is mined and is therefore stale against the actual pool state at execution; and (3) no expiry/deadline is enforced. An MEV searcher seeing the queued pool() transaction can sandwich it: front-run by swapping sUSDS->phUSD (pushing phUSD relative to sUSDS up), let pool() execute against the now-skewed pool (the unbalanced add is interpreted as more imbalance and the pooler pays a much higher implicit swap fee, receiving less BPT), then back-run by reversing the swap. The extracted value comes out of the dispatcher's BPT (which belongs to the protocol).

Re-validation note (yield-claim-nft-07, HEAD 1bb956c): Diff vs c67d3c9 is purely additive (new migrateMint function appended at lines 335-344; two new constants added; one new import). The pool() and unlockCallback bodies are byte-identical to the report-6 commit; only their line numbers have shifted forward by ~10 lines due to the new constants and import. Finding still applies; location updated.
exploit_path:
Setup: BalancerPoolerV2 holds X sUSDS after a sequence of mints. The authorized pooler bot reads getIdealBPT() at block N, computes minBPT = expected * 99% and submits pool(minBPT, ...) at block N+1.

Attack steps:
1. MEV bot sees the pending pool(...) tx in the mempool with X sUSDS to add unbalanced.
2. MEV bot front-runs: swap phUSD -> sUSDS on the BPT pool, pushing the pool out of balance such that sUSDS becomes 'over-weight'. Because UNBALANCED add semantically subtracts a swap-fee-equivalent for the imbalance the joiner causes, depositing sUSDS into an already sUSDS-heavy pool is taxed more.
3. pool() executes against the skewed pool. The single-sided UNBALANCED add returns substantially fewer BPT than the off-chain quote predicted, but is still >= minBPT if the pooler did not set minBPT tight enough.
4. MEV bot back-runs: reverses the swap (sUSDS -> phUSD), pocketing the price impact.

Who profits: MEV searcher. Loss is borne by the protocol (fewer BPT minted to the dispatcher than fair).

Magnitude: On a $10M-depth sUSDS/phUSD pool, a $250k pool() execution can leak 0.05-0.2% (~$125-$500). On a thinner pool (<$2M depth) or larger pool() amount, the leak grows superlinearly.
mainnet_realism: Balancer V3 implements UNBALANCED adds via computeAddLiquidityUnbalanced (BasePoolMath.sol), which explicitly charges a swap fee on the imbalance amount and returns BPT net of that fee. This is exactly the mechanic an attacker exploits. Single-sided LP MEV against Balancer V2/V3 weighted and composable-stable pools is well documented.
recommendation: (a) replace AddLiquidityKind.UNBALANCED with PROPORTIONAL adds; (b) read the pool's current spot via Vault.getPoolTokens / pool-token rate-provider and revert if the spot deviates from the rate-provider price by more than a tight threshold (e.g., 25bps); (c) move pool() execution to a private mempool / commit-reveal. Also: add a deadline parameter to pool().
severity_rationale: Carry-forward from report-6 (Medium). Vulnerability is real value leakage to MEV searchers via sandwich attacks on a single-sided UNBALANCED Balancer V3 addLiquidity. The function is permissioned via onlyAuthorizedPooler, meaning only the protocol's operator bot calls it; the operator can mitigate by using a private mempool. The on-chain code does not enforce this, so the leakage is realistic if operator submits publicly. Medium per C4: value leak with stated external requirement (public mempool submission).
poc_notes: PoC from report-6 still applies — the pool() and unlockCallback function bodies are byte-identical at HEAD 1bb956c vs c67d3c9; only line numbers shifted forward by ~10 due to the new constants and import added for migrateMint. Original PoC: forked mainnet at block 25134513, baseline BPT 528.9e18 vs sandwiched BPT 425.9e18 (19.46% BPT haircut, ~194.6 sUSDS-equivalent value lost). Attacker net sUSDS profit: 181.9e18 on 3000 sUSDS capital.
